doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
title: Why Mandel disliked television writing
summary: Mandel considers television inferior to film and the graveyard of composers like Duane Tatro and Earle Hagen, and they chat about Hagen's Harlem Nocturne.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: [laughs] So, after you did that score, you did quite a bit of television writing then subsequently.

Only as much as I had to, I never liked writing television. I always considered it a far inferior medium to film, budget wise, schedule wise, quality wise, in every way. It was anytime you did TV it was like doing “B” pictures. In fact it took the place of, B, pictures, that’s what happened to, “B” pictures, in-case anybody wants to know.
[they both laugh]
It's interesting, I got to know, do you know Duane Tatro?
Sure, good boy.
As you know he basically made his career writing for television and…
A lot of guys did, never left television.
For some reason he was never able to crack film.
Very hard to make the transition sometimes, that's why I tried to stay away from television, I did not want to end up in the television graveyards, plus I just didn’t like doing the work.
That was the same, the same could be said of Earle Hagen for example, he did mostly television right?
Yeah, yeah he did, that’s true and very well I might add, very inventive composer, did a lot of those good things like, “Mod Squad,” and…
“I Spy.”
“I Spy,” all those things, he wrote interesting stuff.
He used to give a lot of seminars for film and TV composers didn’t he?
Is Earle still around?
I'm not sure I haven't heard anything about him…
In years I haven’t…
In several years yeah.
Good man, he was a lot older than I was.
He wrote, “Harlem Nocturne,” in the late 30s.
He did?
Yeah.
I don’t know why I always thought Alfred Newman did that, I used to get it mixed up with, “Street Song,” I guess, which was Newman's, or, “Street Scene.” They all had that 30s New York sound.
Right, with an alto saxophone.
You bet.
[They both laugh]
Oh, so Earle wrote “Harlem Nocturne,” good piece.
